value.overview: The Yellow-winged Flatbill (Tolmomyias flavotectus) is a small tyrant flycatcher of humid forests in southern Central America and northwestern South America. It was formerly treated as part of the Yellow-margined Flatbill complex, but is now recognized as a separate species. Its broad, flattened bill, olive upperparts, grayish head, pale eye-ring, and conspicuous yellow edging on the wings are useful identification features. It usually stays within forest vegetation and is more often detected by its sharp, emphatic vocalizations than by prolonged views.
value.classification: The Yellow-winged Flatbill belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Tolmomyias. Its scientific name is Tolmomyias flavotectus; it was formerly treated as a subspecies of Tolmomyias assimilis.
value.identification: This flatbill is about 13 cm long and has a large, broad bill typical of the genus. Adults have a dark grayish head, a distinct pale eye-ring, olive-green back and tail, and dusky wings with broad yellow margins that create the characteristic yellow-winged appearance. The throat and breast are pale gray with a yellowish wash, while the belly and undertail coverts are more clearly yellow. The bill is dark above and paler below, and the legs are gray.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Nicaragua through Costa Rica and Panama to western Colombia and northwestern Ecuador, west of the Andes. In Costa Rica it is a resident species occurring on both slopes, especially in humid lowland and foothill forest; it reaches roughly 600 m in northern Costa Rica and about 1,000 m farther south. It uses the interior and edges of wet forest, taller second growth, mature secondary vegetation, swamp forest in parts of its range, and some plantations.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range; it is not considered a long-distance migrant. Local movements may occur, but reliable evidence for regular seasonal migration is lacking.
value.breeding: The breeding season is incompletely known but appears to include at least April through June. The nest is a pear-shaped hanging bag made from fine plant fibers and fungal rhizomorphs, with a tunnel-like entrance that slopes upward toward the lower part of the structure. Nests are suspended from the tip of a branch or vine, commonly several meters above the ground, and may be placed near a wasp nest. Clutch size, incubation, and fledging periods are poorly documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Yellow-winged Flatbill feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, with little fruit thought to be taken. It generally forages alone or in pairs and often joins mixed-species feeding flocks. Most feeding occurs in the middle levels of the forest and toward the canopy, although birds may work lower vegetation along forest edges. Its broad bill is suited to short sallies and gleaning prey from leaves and small branches.
value.behavior: This species is generally unobtrusive and spends much of its time among dense foliage in the forest mid-story and canopy. It frequently participates in mixed-species flocks and may be easier to locate by voice than by sight. The song is a forceful series of short, harsh notes, often delivered from a concealed perch. Singing is reported mainly during the morning and late afternoon. Birds usually occur singly or in pairs outside flocking activity.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size has not been quantified. It is believed to be decreasing, but the species remains fairly common in parts of its range, including Costa Rica, and occurs in protected areas.
